subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Trolley Problem on Wheels
description: A quick win: understand The Trolley Problem on Wheels.

hook.text: If a self-driving car must crash, should it protect its passenger or the pedestrian ahead?

buildup.text: The classic trolley problem becomes real when an AI must choose who gets harmed in a crash.

discovery.text: MIT's Moral Machine survey showed that different cultures make wildly different ethical choices.

twist.text: In practice, engineers say autonomous cars almost never face this choice—they just brake as hard as possible.

climax.text: But the ethical question shapes public trust—people want to know what the car would choose.

punchline.text: The trolley problem rarely happens but always scares people.

quiz.question: What did MIT's Moral Machine survey reveal?
options: All cultures agree on crash ethics
Different cultures make different ethical choices

details.summary: The trolley problem asks whether an autonomous vehicle should swerve to save one group while endangering another, forcing engineers to program ethical decisions that philosophers have debated for centuries.
details.whyItMatters: Programming life-and-death ethical decisions into machines raises profound moral questions about who lives, who dies, and who decides. These dilemmas have no universally accepted answers.
takeaways: Self-driving cars must be programmed for crash-unavoidable scenarios
Different cultures prioritize different lives in ethical surveys
Most AV companies avoid programming explicit ethical choices

faq.question: Do self-driving cars actually face trolley problem scenarios?
faq.answer: In practice, almost never. Real crashes happen too fast for deliberate choices. AV systems prioritize emergency braking and obstacle avoidance rather than choosing between victims. The trolley problem is more philosophical than practical.

faq.question: How did the Moral Machine study contribute to this debate?
faq.answer: MIT's Moral Machine surveyed millions of people worldwide about ethical crash scenarios. Results showed dramatic cultural differences, with some cultures prioritizing the young, others the elderly, complicating any universal solution.
